base_prompt: Explain why deleting a shortcut from a computer's desktop usually does not uninstall the application. A response of around 160 words is enough.
text: A desktop shortcut is usually a small file that points to an application installed elsewhere on your computer. It works like a signpost: clicking it tells the operating system where to find and launch the program, but the shortcut does not contain the application itself. Deleting the shortcut removes only that convenient way of opening the program. The application’s main files, settings, and supporting components remain in their original locations, so you can generally still launch it through the Start menu, an applications folder, a search tool, or another shortcut. Uninstalling is different because it uses a dedicated process to remove the program’s installed files and, where appropriate, related system entries and components. To uninstall an application, you would normally use your operating system’s app management settings or the application’s uninstaller. One important exception is when a desktop item is the actual application rather than a shortcut; deleting that item can remove the program itself, although some associated files may remain.
